notes.b: Every family has more things it wants to do than it has time, money or energy for. Resource management is how a family decides what to do with what it has.
points: Family resource management is using the resources a family has wisely and efficiently to achieve its goals. Resource management is the planned use of the resources available.
A resource is anything a family can draw on to meet its needs and wants, such as a parent's time, a cooker or a weekly wage.
Resources are limited, so choices have to be made about how they are used. This scarcity is why management is needed.

Goals are what the family is trying to achieve, and they give management its direction. Short-term goals include this week's meals or a family outing; long-term goals include buying a home, education or retirement.
notes.tip: If a question asks what family resource management is, give it in one clear sentence: using the family's resources wisely and efficiently to achieve its goals.

notes.b: Managing resources is not only about saving money. The purpose has three parts, and a full answer names all three.
points: The first purpose is to use available resources efficiently in order to achieve goals, so that the family gets the most from what it has.
The second purpose is to improve the quality of family life, so that home is more comfortable and less stressful for everyone.
The third purpose is to enable each family member to reach their full potential, because well-managed time, money and support leave room for learning, work and interests.
Good management reduces waste of time, money, food and energy, and gets the best value from limited resources.
It also avoids conflict and stress by agreeing who does what, so members know what is expected of them.

Example of efficient management: a weekly meal plan with a shopping list saves money and time and reduces food waste, because the family buys only what it will use. Other examples are budgeting, planned childcare, sharing household tasks, or resolving a conflict by agreeing a timetable.
notes.tip: A usual answer gives two purpose points plus one example of efficient management, each linked back to efficiency. Do not give only 'to save money', and keep each point short with a reason or example rather than writing an essay.

notes.b: Families draw on four kinds of resource, and only one of them is money. Naming each type with an example shows you understand what the family has to work with.
points: Human resources: the time, energy, skills and knowledge of family members, such as one parent's cooking skills or a teenager's free afternoon.
Material resources: equipment, food, ingredients, clothing, furniture and other household goods, such as a washing machine or a freezer.
Economic resources: income, savings and credit available to the family.
Environmental resources: the physical surroundings and community facilities that support family life, such as space, daylight and local services like schools, transport and health care.
Resources other than money matter as much as money. A family with little money can still manage well by using time, skills, knowledge and good planning.
notes.tip: Students often write that resources are money. Make clear that time, skills, knowledge, people and equipment count too, and give an example of each type if asked to name them.

notes.b: A management system is a planned, step-by-step way of turning a need or goal into a result using the resources available. In other words, it turns what you have into what you wanted.
points: A management system lets a family decide what needs doing, who does it, when it is done and which resources it needs.

Everyday tasks that use a management system include meal planning, budgeting, housework, childcare and shopping. Money and home management, problem solving and decision-making are also uses of the management process.
One-off events such as a birthday party, a holiday or a house move also use a management system, as does a problem such as choosing an appliance.
Systems work best when the goals, standards and responsibilities are agreed in advance and tasks are shared, so that members know what is expected of them.
Systems are not fixed: they are adjusted when circumstances change, such as a new job, a job loss, a move or the arrival of a baby.
A system is a cycle, not a one-off. The result is checked against the goal, and what was learned improves the next attempt. This checking is called feedback.

notes.h: How good management contributes to a well-run home
notes.b: When a family uses a management system well, the benefits show up in everyday life: in time, money, workload, relationships and the ability to cope with change.
points: Time is used well. Planned routines make sure meals, laundry and school preparation are done on time, with less last-minute stress.
Money is used well. Meal plans and shopping lists reduce impulse buying and the amount of food that is wasted, and budgeting helps the family avoid debt.
Work is shared fairly. Shared tasks spread the workload so no single member carries the whole household, and each member learns skills.
Goals and standards agreed by all members give the family a shared direction, support communication and reduce conflict.
Energy, water and food are used carefully, so the cost of running the home is lower and there is less waste.
Efficient use of time and equipment frees time for leisure, rest and relationships, so quality of life improves.
The family copes better with change and emergencies because it has a plan and some resources in reserve.
notes.tip: Answer in short points, each with a reason or example, such as planned routines, time and money used well, tasks shared, shared goals with less conflict, and more leisure time.

notes.h: The family as a managerial unit
notes.b: The family is a small group that pools, allocates and controls its own resources. Because it sets goals and takes responsibility for results, it acts as a managerial unit.
points: Each member contributes resources such as earnings, time or skills, and each member benefits from the shared pool of the household.
The family sets goals, makes decisions, allocates resources and takes responsibility for the results.
Adults usually plan, earn and coordinate; children and teenagers take on tasks and share in decisions as they grow older. This means management duties are shared and change over time.
Family goals may be short term, such as a weekly shop or a family outing, or long term, such as buying a home or saving for education.
Management requires balancing individual wants against the needs and goals of the household as a whole, so the unit works best when decisions take everyone's views into account.
Article 41 of the Irish Constitution recognises the family as the natural, primary and fundamental unit group of society.
notes.tip: When describing the family as a managerial unit, say it is the group that sets goals, pools resources and shares decisions and tasks.

keyTerms.definition: Anything a family can draw on to meet its needs and wants.
The efficient use of available resources to achieve the goals of the family.
The time, energy, skills and knowledge of the people in a family.
The equipment, food, goods and other physical items a family uses in the home.
The income, savings and credit available to a family to pay for what it needs.
The physical surroundings and community facilities that support family life.
A planned, step-by-step way of turning a need or goal into a result using available resources.
A group, such as the family, that plans and controls its own resources.

questions.prompt: Outline the purpose of family resource management and give one example of how a family can use its resources efficiently.
questions.model: Purpose, any two points at 2 marks each (4 marks): to use available resources efficiently in order to achieve goals; to improve the quality of family life; to enable each family member to reach their full potential. Example (2 marks): a weekly meal plan with a shopping list uses money and time efficiently and reduces food waste.

questions.prompt: Discuss how a family, acting as a managerial unit, uses its resources to achieve its goals. Refer to the types of resource and to the goals a family may set in your answer.
questions.model: Family as a managerial unit: the family pools its income, time, skills and goods and decides how they are allocated. Types of resource: human (time, energy, skills, knowledge), material (equipment, food, goods), economic (income, savings, credit) and environmental (space, facilities, surroundings). Goals: short term, such as a weekly shop or an outing, and long term, such as buying a home or saving for education. Process: adults plan and coordinate; children and teenagers take on tasks and share in decisions as they grow older. Management system: tasks, responsibilities and standards are agreed in advance and the plan is adjusted when circumstances change. Balance: individual wants must be weighed against the needs and goals of the household as a whole. Outcome: resources are used efficiently, waste is reduced and the quality of family life improves.
